newsitem.title: BELGIUM: European Parliament makes measured use of powers.
newsitem.headline: European Parliament makes measured use of powers.

text.p: After a series of embarrassing climbdowns the European Parliament finally flexed its muscles this week, using the public health scare over mad cow disease to assert itself at a time when it is seeking more powers.

The assembly stopped short of firing the European Commission on the spot on Thursday for mishandling the bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE) outbreak, but a day earlier voted to put it on nine-months' notice to put things right or be out of a job.
It was the fourth time in seven years that the parliament had voted on a motion censuring the commission -- a vote which if it is carried forces the EU executive to resign.
Two in 1990 and 1991 garnered fewer than 20 votes and a third in 1992 picked up 96 votes. Thursday's vote was backed by 118 members but 326 voted against.

A four-month parliamentary committee of inquiry, which condemned both the EU executive and the British government for mishandling the crisis, extracted a promise of action from Commission President Jacques Santer and a proposal of new powers, which the parliament is desperately seeking.

French Socialist Elisabeth Guigou, one of two parliament representatives on the EU's inter-governmental treaty review, said in a statement the committee had helped pinpoint those responsible and propose concrete steps to avoid future crises.
Santer promised a shake-up of the Commission's services to take health policy away from its agriculture division and offered the parliament a right of veto over EU health policy.
Relieved Commission officials said Santer had held on to his job by telling the parliament exactly what it had wanted to hear -- that they could have more powers.
The problem is, this is not in Santer's gift. It is up to EU governments which are unlikely to concur during the institutional review set to wind up in Amsterdam in June.
Commission officials said that the measures demanded by the parliament had been watered down to remove the most difficult to accomplish and leave only what was palatable and practicable.
Some deputies lamented the measured approach of the parliament, saying it should have fired the Commission outright.

"It shows parliament is like Popeye without spinach," French Socialist Andre Laignel said, adding that like the cartoon character, the assembly liked to show its muscles but lacked the courage to take action.
Others said that in adopting a measured approach -- rather than crying wolf as in the past -- it had secured change.

While the parliament is seen as having dealt responsibly with new legislative co-decision powers granted under the Maastricht Treaty, often negotiating from a position of weakness, when it comes to major institutional and political questions it has often failed to follow up on threats.
In May 1994 the parliament, seeking to wrest new powers from the EU, threatened to block the entry of four new members to the EU and then voted them in by a landslide.

In July 1994 it ranted and raved about the backroom deal between EU governments which put then Luxembourg Prime Minister Santer at the head of the the Commission until 2000. Then, under pressure from national capitals, it narrowly voted him in.

Barely had the dust settled than in January 1995 the parliament threatened to use one of its only effective powers and refuse to accept the new Commission, after finding one Commissioner in four wanting in confirmation hearings.
But again it backtracked.
In December 1995, it threatened to veto a lucrative customs union between the EU and Turkey, only to set its human rights concerns aside to usher in the money-spinning deal.
This week, however, the parliament had its day.

Even so, some members muttered that a nine-month grace period was ill-timed, as the parliament might not be willing to fire the Commisssion just before the start of a crucial period in the EU's plans for economic and monetary union.
In the unlikely event that Santer fails to fulfil his promises, they said, the parliament could have set itself up to cry wolf again.
